title: Decoupled Reservation and Preemptive Fallthrough for Dedicated Capacity
creator: Marisol Chen
description: Problem statement: Customers running latency-sensitive workloads on Dedicated capacity observe occasional request failures or severe latency spikes when shared autoscale and burst policies preempt reserved allocations. This PRD proposes decoupling the reservation accounting path from opportunistic burst/autoscale allocations and adding a preemptive fallthrough policy so critical reserved traffic gracefully shifts to a predictable fallback (compatible model variant, warmed preemption pool, or transient hosted lane) instead of failing outright.
background: Current Dedicated capacity implementation mixes reserved slot accounting with opportunistic burst buckets. When cluster pressure triggers eviction, we see two customer-facing issues: 1) reserved requests get delayed or rejected because eviction prioritizes node compaction; 2) heuristic fallbacks are inconsistent across regions causing customer confusion and SE escalations. Prior incident INC-2024-11 called out a major customer outage where a large peak triggered cascading preemptions and the reserved queue experienced 7x latency degradation for 23 minutes. Root causes: tight coupling of reservation lifecycle and autoscale allocator, no prioritized fallthrough route, and insufficient telemetry to drive per-tenant decisioning.
goals: Introduce a decoupled reservation accounting path so reserved commitments are tracked independently from opportunistic burst allocations
Implement a deterministic preemptive fallthrough policy that routes reserved traffic to a safe fallback under capacity contention
Provide operator controls and observability: per-tenant fallthrough thresholds, audit events, and SLO-aligned fallback selection
Minimize customer-visible failures—success criterion: reduce reserved-request rejections by 95% under modeled peak contention scenarios
non_goals: Full rewrite of the autoscaler or placement engine—this is an incremental architectural change
Solving long-term capacity forecasting—this PRD focuses on runtime decisioning and fallbacks
Addressing on-prem orchestration differences for air-gapped installs in this phase (will be tracked separately)
scope: API-level: new reservation status flag and fallthrough policy configuration in Dedicated API/console
Runtime: split accounting tables for reserved vs burst; routing policy to select fallback lane
Console/Telemetry: dashboard panels for reserved failover events, per-tenant fallthrough counts, and latency distribution post-fallback
Operator UX: emergency override to force-failover or pause fallthrough for debugging
acceptance_criteria: Configuration: Customers can set per-reservation fallthrough policy (options: warm-preempt-pool, compatible-variant, hosted-fallback, fail) via API and console
Runtime: Under synthetic contention test, reserved requests are not rejected and are routed to configured fallback within configured SLA 99th latency for 95% of requests
Observability: Telemetry emits events for every fallthrough decision with tenant_id, reservation_id, reason_code, chosen_fallback, and latency_post_fallback
Auditability: Admins can query fallthrough history for a tenant for 90 days
Operator controls: On-call can toggle global fallthrough enable/disable and adjust thresholds without a restart
Docs & SDK: SDKs expose new reservation status and fallthrough options; console docs and runbook updated
success_metrics: Reserved-request rejection rate during peak windows reduced by >=95% compared to baseline
Customer SE tickets tied to reservation preemption reduced by >=80% within 60 days of rollout
Median latency for fallthrough path within 2x baseline median latency and p99 within SLO for 95% of tenants
Feature adoption: >=30% of active reserved tenants enable non-fail fallthrough within first 90 days
rollout_plan: Phase 0 - Design & spike (2 weeks): infra spike to validate split accounting and basic policy hooks
Phase 1 - Internal dogfood (3 weeks): enable decoupled accounting in staging, route a small percentage of reserved traffic via warm-preempt-pool fallback
Phase 2 - Canary (4 weeks): 2-3 low-risk customers in production with observability and on-call guardrails
Phase 3 - Gradual rollout (6 weeks): progressive percentage ramp and region-by-region enablement
Phase 4 - Full GA and docs (2 weeks): public docs, Console UI enablement, and deprecation of older fallback heuristics
open_questions: Which fallback should be the default for new customers: compatible-variant or hosted-fallback? We need cost and privacy tradeoffs for hosted-fallback.
What are acceptable latency SLOs for each fallback option? Engineering to propose realistic targets for warm-preempt vs hosted-fallback.
Should fallthrough events count against customer billing quotas? Finance + Legal input required.
For Private/VPC deployments, is hosted-fallback allowed or must we restrict to compatible-variant only?
decisions: Decouple accounting: approved—split reservations and burst in allocator database (Liam O'Connor, 2025-02-20)
Telemetry contract: emit fallthrough events with standardized reason_code (Aisha Patel, 2025-02-25)
Default policy: use compatible-variant as conservative default for GA; allow hosted-fallback opt-in (Marisol Chen, 2025-02-28)
updates: 2025-02-18: Kickoff meeting—aligned on goals, high-level architecture and test plan. Action: ENG spike requested (ENG- spike created)
2025-02-24: Engineering spike complete; proof-of-concept shows decoupled counters reduce allocator churn in staging. Found missing TTL on reservation snapshot; ENG to patch.
2025-02-26: Security triage—hosted-fallback flagged for additional privacy review for PII-sensitive tenants. Security assigned follow-up (ticket SEC-482).
2025-03-01: Design review—console mockups for per-reservation policy controls approved with minor UX updates (DES-809). Diego to iterate on confirmation copy.
2025-03-02: PM review—updated acceptance criteria to require 90-day auditability window and explicit billing decision before GA. Follow-up: Finance sync 2025-03-04.
notes: Trade-offs: compatible-variant fallback is lowest risk for privacy but may increase latency or cost; hosted-fallback offers most predictable latency but requires strong data-handling guarantees. We prioritize correctness and auditability over a minimal-latency first release. Implementation should be incremental and well-instrumented for rollback.
